pages.x: Two and a half centuries after the conquest, the native peoples of the Andes were still forced to work in the silver mines of Potosí under the mita, a labour draft that sent many to their deaths, and to buy goods at high prices from Spanish officials, the corregidores. New taxes in the 1770s made things worse.

José Gabriel Condorcanqui, a wealthy mule-train owner and local chief, was descended from Túpac Amaru, the last Inca ruler, executed by the Spanish in 1572, and took the name Túpac Amaru II. On 4 November 1780 his men seized the hated corregidor Antonio de Arriaga, and six days later hanged him.

His wife, Micaela Bastidas, ran the rebels' supplies and recruiting, and urged him to strike at Cusco before the Spanish could gather their forces. He waited. By the time tens of thousands of rebels laid siege to the old Inca capital in January 1781, it had been reinforced, and the siege failed.

In April 1781 Túpac Amaru was betrayed and captured. On 18 May, in the main square of Cusco, he was made to watch the execution of his wife and son. Then his tongue was cut out, and horses were tied to his arms and legs to tear him apart. When they failed, he was beheaded.

The rising went on. In the south an Aymara leader, Túpac Katari, besieged La Paz for months in 1781, and thousands inside died of hunger. He too was captured and torn apart by horses. Before he died, he is remembered as saying: I will return, and I will be millions.

By the time the last rebels gave up in 1782, perhaps 100,000 people had died, most of them native Andeans. Spain banned the titles and dress of the Inca nobility, and even the Quechua plays that told of the Incas.

pages.x: The rising failed, but it was the greatest revolt in Spain's American empire before the wars of independence forty years later. Túpac Amaru became a symbol of resistance across Latin America, and the name of the Inca rebel lives on in Peru and beyond.
